description: The lead single from the Nashville band's 2024 EP This Could All Go Nowhere — a soulful, sunny-sounding confession about being too afraid of your own feelings to say them out loud.

pops.text: This is the lead single — and opening track — of the band's 2024 EP This Could All Go Nowhere. First impressions, delivered as a warning.

The band's own summary is brutally honest: it's about being afraid of your feelings, bottling them up, and hoping the other person acts first. 'The bad bad news is that I can't do what I need to do myself.'
Notice the trick: that heavy confession rides on happy music. The band calls that mismatch 'classic B&B.'
Underneath is a soulful drum-and-bass groove with sunny, cascading vocals — frontman Joseph Settine pleading 'let me down easy' at the center of it.
It was the group's first release since their 2023 album Bluebeard, ending a year-long wait with a three-minute single.
The EP arrived November 14, 2024 via AWAL — five tracks, about 18 minutes, all warmth on the surface and ache underneath.
Settine calls the whole EP a 'happy accident': five songs recorded with no strings attached, just to be in the studio making things together.
Band-name geography: Settine grew up in Birmingham's Bluff Park and guitarist Alec Bolton in Mountain Brook. The Brook & The Bluff is literally home, split in two.
The two founded the band in 2015, in their senior year at Auburn University. It started as an acoustic duo before growing into the harmony-stacked five-piece you hear here.
They took this material out supporting Stephen Sanchez and Rainbow Kitten Surprise in fall 2024 — a fitting bill for a song that's all sunshine outside, storm inside.

title: Bad Bad News

description: Ric Ocasek wrote it, bassist Benjamin Orr sang it, and Live Aid made it immortal — the Cars' biggest hit, a synth-drenched ballad from 1984's Heartbeat City.

pops.text: Ric Ocasek wrote this one, but he handed the microphone to bassist Benjamin Orr. Orr's warmer, more vulnerable voice is the whole heart of the record.
Released July 23, 1984, it was the third single from Heartbeat City, the Cars' fifth album — after 'You Might Think' and 'Magic' had already hit.
It became the Cars' highest-charting US single: No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 1 on the Adult Contemporary chart.
The polish is producer Robert John 'Mutt' Lange's — fresh off Def Leppard's Pyromania, he co-produced Heartbeat City with the band.
The director was an actor: Oscar winner Timothy Hutton. He lived next door to Cars manager Elliot Roberts, raved about the unreleased song, and got asked to direct his concept.
Hutton filmed over two days at Astoria Studios in New York. Spot the band as tuxedo-clad mannequins, posed with their instruments in a deserted nightclub.
The woman in the video is 19-year-old model Paulina Porizkova, playing Ocasek's unraveling girlfriend. She and Ocasek later married — the video is where they met.
At Live Aid in July 1985, David Bowie introduced a famine montage at Wembley that used 'Drive' as its music. Viewers never forgot the pairing.
The Cars played it live hours later in Philadelphia, with Orr singing. Re-released in the UK, it climbed back to No. 4 in August 1985.

Proceeds from that re-release raised nearly £160,000 for the Band Aid Trust — Ocasek personally handed the cheque to trustee Midge Ure in 1986. Covers followed from Deftones and Ziggy Marley, whose version appears in 50 First Dates.

title: Drive

description: A jangle-pop anti-war gem from Raleigh's own Connells — track seven on 1987's Boylan Heights, complete with an ironic military trumpet drifting through the chorus.

pops.text: Raleigh royalty: the Connells formed in spring 1984 around brothers Mike Connell (guitar) and David Connell (bass), with Doug MacMillan singing lead.
This is track seven on Boylan Heights, the band's second album, released in 1987 — every song on it was written by Mike Connell except 'Home Today.'
Hear that trumpet? It's an ironic military trumpet counter-melody woven into an anti-war song — the album credits the trumpet to Bill Spencer.
The album is named for a real place: Boylan Heights, the historic Raleigh neighborhood. Hometown pride, right on the cover.
Producer Mitch Easter recorded it at his Drive-In Studio in Winston-Salem, North Carolina — the epicenter of the Southern jangle-pop scene.
Mike Connell remembers the sessions starting in March 1987 — and the band pausing to play party gigs to earn more money to pay for the record.
Boylan Heights was their first album for TVT Records — after major labels, including Columbia, had passed on it. Their loss.
Trouser Press heard Mike Connell's songs as 'yearning collegiate considerations of love, war and alienation.' 'Over There' is the war entry.
MusicHound Rock later called Boylan Heights 'one of the most distinctive college rock albums of the '80s,' and it was a substantial college-radio hit.
Decades on, it's still a live staple — it featured in the band's appearance on PBS North Carolina's Shaped By Sound series, Raleigh boys playing a Raleigh song for North Carolina.

title: Over There

description: The opening stomp of 1974's Southern Comfort — a five-minute-plus instrumental where trombone, tenor sax, clavinet and Larry Carlton's guitar turn jazz into pure funk.

pops.text: No singer, no problem: this is a pure instrumental, and it opens the Crusaders' 1974 album Southern Comfort with a stomp, as promised.
It was written by trombonist Wayne Henderson — one half of the band's signature front line, his trombone locked in with Wilton Felder's tenor saxophone.
The band's roots run deep: pianist Joe Sample, Felder and drummer Stix Hooper started playing together as Houston high-schoolers in a 1954 group called the Swingsters.
For a decade they were the Jazz Crusaders, a hard-bop outfit. In 1971 they dropped the word 'Jazz' from the name — deliberately, so it wouldn't limit their audience.
Southern Comfort was the first of their Blue Thumb albums distributed by ABC Records, a bigger stage for a band crossing over.
It was also the album cycle where guitarist Larry Carlton became a full-fledged member, adding a lyrical sting to the funk.
Joe Sample's keyboards do heavy lifting here — electric piano and clavinet were now central to the sound that made the 'Jazz' in their old name too small.
As a single in 1975, this instrumental still charted: No. 41 on the US R&B chart and No. 12 on the US Dance chart. Funk needs no lyrics.
The album itself was a smash: No. 1 on Billboard's Jazz LPs chart, No. 3 on Soul LPs and No. 31 on the overall Top LPs chart.
Henderson left in 1975 to produce, so this is the classic lineup near its peak — five years before 'Street Life' with Randy Crawford gave them their biggest pop hit.

title: Stomp And Buck Dance

description: The opening blast of Electric (1987), the album the Cult recorded twice — Rick Rubin stripped their gothic swirl down to AC/DC-sized riffs, and this flower got loud.

pops.text: This opens Electric, the Cult's third album — and it announces the new sound in seconds: one huge riff, pounding drums, Ian Astbury howling over the top.
It's written by the band's two constants, singer Ian Astbury and guitarist Billy Duffy — the partnership at the center of every Cult lineup.
You are hearing take two of an album. The Cult first recorded these songs as Peace at the Manor Studios with Love producer Steve Brown — then scrapped the whole thing.
Two months of work went in the bin because the band found it too polished. Producer Rick Rubin agreed to help only if they re-recorded — so they re-recorded everything.
Rubin was a hip-hop producer, Def Jam's co-founder, fresh off Run-D.M.C. and the Beastie Boys. Hiring him to remake a gothic rock band was the gamble that paid off.
The re-recording happened in New York, and the sound is deliberate: sparse, dry and riff-first, with Rubin's hip-hop ear emphasizing the bass drum.
Electric reached No. 4 in the UK and spent 27 weeks on the chart — the longest chart run of any Cult album — and became their first US Top 40 album.
'Wild Flower' was the album's third single, released in the summer of 1987 after 'Love Removal Machine' and 'Lil' Devil.' Even its B-side reached back to the scrapped Peace sessions.
On the North American tour, the opening band was Guns N' Roses — invited personally by Astbury, who had caught them in London and raved about them to Duffy.
Fans finally heard both albums side by side in 2013, when the reissue Electric Peace paired Rubin's version with the long-shelved Peace recordings.

title: Wild Flower

description: The Cure's bright, jangly 1979 single about a boy who blew it and won't admit he's crying about it. A flop on first release, it became one of the band's signature songs.

pops.text: Released as a standalone UK single on 12 June 1979, this wasn't on the Cure's British debut album at all. America got it as the title track of the US version, Boys Don't Cry, in 1980.
Label boss Chris Parry was sure this was a Top 10 hit — he said so in the band biography Ten Imaginary Years. On release in 1979, it didn't chart in the UK at all.
Robert Smith was just 20 when this came out. The band was still a trio: Smith, bassist Michael Dempsey and drummer Lol Tolhurst.
Smith told Rolling Stone in 2019 that English boys were 'encouraged not to show your emotion to any degree' — and that he 'couldn't help' showing his. That tension is the whole song.
The B-side of the original single was 'Plastic Passion.' The 1986 B-sides, including 'Pillbox Tales,' were remastered for a 2026 anniversary EP.
Second chance, 1986: Smith re-sang the vocal and remixed the track — billed 'New Voice, New Mix' — to promote the singles collection Standing on a Beach. This time it reached No. 22 in the UK.
The video you're watching is the 1986 one, directed by Tim Pope. Child actors mime the song as the original trio, while the adult band looms in silhouette behind a curtain, eyes glowing.
Billboard ranked this No. 4 on its 2019 list of the 40 greatest Cure songs, and Mojo put it at No. 3 on its 2023 list of the band's 30 greatest. Not bad for a non-charting single.
The title was borrowed for the acclaimed 1999 film Boys Don't Cry, starring Hilary Swank — a very different, much darker story sharing this song's name.
In January 2026 this became the first Cure song ever to pass one billion streams on Spotify — nearly 47 years after it first missed the charts completely.

title: Boys Don't Cry

description: The Go-Go's' sun-soaked 1982 title track — a postcard from a holiday romance you already regret leaving. It peaked at No. 8 and became their second and final US Top 10 hit.

pops.text: Bassist Kathy Valentine wrote the first version years earlier, after a brief holiday romance — she started the lyrics on the plane ride home, per Ultimate Classic Rock.
This song had a first life: Valentine's earlier band the Textones released their version in the UK on Chiswick Records in 1980, two years before the Go-Go's hit.
For the Go-Go's version, Charlotte Caffey and Jane Wiedlin joined Valentine as co-writers, and Richard Gottehrer produced. It led off their second album, also called Vacation.
Format history: 'Vacation' was the first known cassette single — the 'cassingle,' trademarked by I.R.S. Records — released in the United States.
The flip side of the 7-inch was 'Beatnik Beach,' a surf-rock number. Keep the beach theme going, flip the record over.
It peaked at No. 8 on the Billboard Hot 100 in August 1982 — the Go-Go's' second Top 10 hit, and, as it turned out, their final one in the US.
The video was directed by Mick Haggerty and C.D. Taylor and shot in a single day on a $50,000 budget — big money for a music video in 1982.
That water-skiing finale recreates the album cover — and it was faked with blue screen. The band starts on a pile of airport luggage and ends as a photo in a travel brochure.
The champagne was real. Jane Wiedlin admitted the band drank lots of it during the shoot: by the water-ski scenes, she said, 'we're all like cross-eyed drunk.'
Decades later, the song earned a Broadway credit: it was included in Head Over Heels, the Go-Go's jukebox musical that opened on Broadway in 2018.

title: Vacation

description: A hazy soul ballad from Brighton duo The Heavy Heavy — the first song Will Turner and Georgie Fuller ever recorded together, first released on their 2020 debut EP Life and Life Only.

pops.text: This is where it started: ATO Records calls 'Go Down River' the first song Will Turner and Georgie Fuller ever recorded together as The Heavy Heavy.
Turner had carried the song around unfinished for a while. He told The Current that once Fuller added her vocals, 'it all came together' — the male-female harmonies created their sound.
Turner's review of the finished track: it 'just felt like lying in the green grass on a hot sunny day.' The lyric video is happy to go along with that.
The pair formed The Heavy Heavy in the autumn of 2019, though they'd met almost seven years earlier working on other people's musical projects.
They self-produced their debut EP, Life and Life Only, in a London flat. This song sat alongside 'Miles and Miles,' 'All My Dreams' and 'Man of the Hills.'
The EP first came out in 2020, in the middle of lockdown, after the band had managed just two acoustic gigs. ATO Records picked it up and reissued an expanded version in 2022.
Their stated mission: 'making records that sound like our favorite records ever.' Turner even tracked the old way — he told Magnet he tries to record with eight tracks, as it was done back then.
Asked for their sound in one line, the band told NME: the Rolling Stones meet The Mamas & The Papas — 'The Stones are the bottom of everything we do,' Turner said.
Fuller is a classically trained singer who performed at the Montreux Jazz Festival as a teenager; Turner hails from Malvern, the countryside town he hymns in 'Man of the Hills.'
Asked his favourite of their own songs in a Holler interview, Turner picked this one: 'Go Down River.' The EP's music later turned up in shows including Outer Range and Superman & Lois.

title: Go Down River

description: The Meters' 1969 instrumental masterclass in New Orleans funk — no singer, no wasted notes, just guitar, bass, organ and Zigaboo Modeliste's drums strutting for three minutes.

pops.text: No words at all — and it still went Top 40. This 1969 instrumental reached No. 23 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 4 on the R&B chart.
Guitarist Leo Nocentelli wrote it as a new set opener, because he was tired of opening with 'Hold It,' a tune lots of bands used. At first, his replacement didn't even have a name.
'We started opening the set with it, but it didn't have a name or anything,' Nocentelli told Gibson. It was named 'Cissy Strut' long after he wrote it.
The writing credit is shared by all four Meters: Nocentelli, Art Neville on organ, George Porter Jr. on bass and drummer Joseph 'Zigaboo' Modeliste. Producers: Allen Toussaint and Marshall Sehorn.
Listen to the hook: guitar and bass play the lead melody in unison — an early pop hit built that way — while Neville's organ and Modeliste's second-line drums leave those famous gaps of air.
The Meters were Allen Toussaint's house band in New Orleans, backing singers like Lee Dorsey and Dr. John by day and cutting instrumentals like this under their own name.
The Meters' catalogue became one of hip-hop's favourite sample sources, borrowed by acts including A Tribe Called Quest, Public Enemy, LL Cool J, EPMD and Queen Latifah.
Quentin Tarantino slipped this into his 1997 film Jackie Brown — it's heard in the movie, though it didn't make the commercially released soundtrack album.
In 2011, 'Cissy Strut' was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame, honouring recordings of lasting significance at least 25 years old. The band itself got a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2018.
In 2021 Rolling Stone ranked this No. 158 on its 500 Greatest Songs of All Time — a rare instrumental on the list, and a fixture every funk band is still expected to know.

title: Cissy Strut

description: The opening track of The Motet's 2004 album Music for Life — six-plus minutes of Colorado funk from drummer Dave Watts' band, all brass, organ and a rhythm section that won't sit down.

pops.text: Track one, side one: 'Cheap Shit' opens The Motet's 2004 album Music for Life, released on Harmonized Records — the label that had put out their live album two years earlier.
The Motet is drummer Dave Watts' band. He founded it in Boulder, Colorado in 1998 as a rotating musical collective; the first Dave Watts Motet show was on Halloween 1998.
Watts was the principal songwriter on most of Music for Life, but JamBands' review stressed he mostly used his tunes as launchpads for his bandmates' improvisations.
That guitar work is Mark Donovan. The review singled out his 'bold, melodic skronk' riding over the no-frills rhythm section of Watts and bassist Garrett Sayers.
Trading riffs over the top: tenor and alto saxophonists Dominic Lalli and Jon Stewart with keyboardist Greg Raymond — JamBands compared their exchanges to schoolboys trading jokes.
The album's recipe, per that same review: take it and 'boil it down' and nothing boils off — 'clean, untainted, fresh jazz, distilled to its funkiest essence.'
Another reviewer, hearing this track on the Pure Hemp 'One Love' compilation, called it 'a pounding funk exercise drenched with saucy organ, brilliant brass, and smooth bass.'
In the summer of 2004 the band toured the West Coast to support Music for Life — and ran its tour bus on biodiesel made from vegetable oil, per a JamBands report at the time.
Watts came to funk with formal training: he studied at Berklee College of Music in Boston before his earlier band Shockra and, later, The Motet.
The song stayed in the live arsenal for years: at Florida's AURA festival in 2015, The Motet closed their set by bringing 'Cheap Shit' back as the encore.

title: Cheap Shit

description: An uptempo, tambourine-driven soul-jazz instrumental from Old School, the Leeds funk quartet's 18th album — Hammond organ up front, echo-tinged guitar in reply, and a rhythm section locked in tight.

pops.text: No warm-up lap here: 'Smoothie' is track four of ten on Old School, and reviewers say it 'bolts out of the gate with all four chugging along.'
FunkCity's track-by-track verdict: 'Uptempo tambourine-driven souljazz somewhere between Boogaloo Joe Jones and early JTQ but with a much crunchier drum sound.'
That's Joe Tatton carrying the main melody on sustained organ chords. Old School is a Hammond B3-heavy album, and Tatton — who joined in 2007 — is its featured player.
Listen in stereo: Eddie Roberts takes an echo-tinged guitar solo mostly in the left channel, then Tatton's pulsing organ answers from the right.
The core four, unchanged for years: Roberts on guitar, Pete Shand on bass, Simon Allen on drums and Tatton on keys. That consistency is the band's calling card.
The band formed in Leeds, England in 1999, when guitarist and producer Eddie Roberts was running a club night there called The Cooker devoted to classic soul and funk.
Old School was the group's 18th LP, released March 29, 2024 — 25 years after they started. Drummer Simon Allen joked the tracks are 'all new songs — but they sound like our old songs.'
Two labels, one band: Old School came out on One Note Records in the UK and Europe — the label Allen has run since 2003 — and via Roberts' Color Red in the US.
Hungry? Old School is full of food titles — 'Breakfast T,' 'Do the Sausage Roll' and this 'Smoothie.' One Fillmore review wondered if the band was famished when they wrote them.
On stage, 'Smoothie' is usually served with its neighbor: 2024 setlists repeatedly pair it back-to-back with the next album track, 'Two Fat Ladies (88).'

title: Smoothie

description: The title track of the Finnish soul outfit's 2009 album Soup Is Hot — a five-minute R&B/soul groove from a nine-track record issued in Finland on the Jupiter label.

pops.text: Yes, the soup is also the album: this is the title track of Soup Is Hot, sitting at track three of nine.
The Soultwisters are a Finnish group — MusicBrainz lists their home country as Finland, and the album was released there in 2009.
The album came out on Jupiter, and the cataloguers file it under R&B/Soul — deep-groove territory, not pop-chart territory.
Clock it: at 5:11, this is the album's second-longest track. Only 'Clyde,' at 5:17, runs longer.
Vinyl buyers got it on side A: on the original 12-inch LP, 'Soup Is Hot' is track A3, after 'Soulpudding' and 'The Floor.'
The album opens with 'Soulpudding' and closes with 'Baker's Song' — somebody in this band was thinking about the kitchen a lot.
More menu energy elsewhere on the record: 'Tequila Afternoon.' Between that and the hot soup, it's a full tasting menu in nine tracks.
MusicBrainz dates the first release of the album's recordings to February 24, 2009 — a winter release for a record called Soup Is Hot. Appropriate.
There was never a music video for this one. The version you're hearing is the official audio served to YouTube through the band's Topic channel.
The streaming edition keeps the vinyl's nine-track shape: 'Soulpudding' first, 'Soup Is Hot' third, and 'Baker's Song' — a 5:08 closer — last.

title: Soup Is Hot

description: The sunny-on-the-surface opener of Loaded (1970), Lou Reed's heartbreak song sung by Doug Yule — the Velvets' most pop-oriented single, ba-ba-bas and all, from their final album with Reed.

pops.text: This is track one of Loaded — and the first voice you hear isn't Lou Reed's. Reed wrote the song, but Doug Yule sings lead.
Loaded was the band's fourth studio album, released November 15, 1970 on Cotillion, Atlantic Records' subsidiary label.

The title was a gag: Atlantic asked for an album 'loaded with hits,' so the band called it Loaded and pushed for a hit single. Yule recalled the big question was which song could be cut down to single length.
'Who Loves the Sun' was issued as Loaded's first single, backed with another Yule-sung track, 'Oh! Sweet Nuthin''.'
Yule was Loaded's secret weapon: he sings lead on four of its ten songs — this one, 'New Age,' 'Lonesome Cowboy Bill' and 'Oh! Sweet Nuthin''.'
Drummer Maureen Tucker is credited on the sleeve but never plays on the album — she was on maternity leave. The drums on this track were played by recording engineer Adrian Barber.
By the time you could buy Loaded, its songwriter was gone: Reed left the Velvet Underground on August 23, 1970, about three months before the album came out.
Original LP copies have a party trick: there's no silence between this song and 'Sweet Jane' — the next track's first note lands the instant this one finishes fading.
Despite the sunshine-pop sheen and those Beach Boys-style 'ba ba ba' backing vocals, the single didn't chart. The hit Atlantic wanted never arrived.
The song kept cooking, though: Rhino's 1997 Fully Loaded reissue included an alternate mix running 3:08, noticeably longer than the original 2:47.

title: Who Loves the Sun

description: The Who's 1972 non-album single, written by Pete Townshend for the abandoned Lifehouse project — a join-the-band singalong built on synthesizer, Jew's harp and two kinds of harmonica.

pops.text: This was a standalone single, not an album track: released June 16, 1972 in the UK on Track Records, and July 8 in the US on Decca.
Pete Townshend wrote it for Lifehouse, his never-finished rock opera. It was the second of three non-album singles tied to that abandoned project.

Roger Daltrey swears Townshend 'literally wrote it the night before we recorded it.' The band cut it in a single day — May 22, 1972 — at Olympic Studios in London, with Glyn Johns as associate producer.
Daltrey was skeptical of the new toy: he recalled doubting the synthesizer, figuring the band would spend ages making 'piddly one-note noises' better done on guitar.
Chart report: No. 9 in the UK and No. 17 on the US Billboard Hot 100. Townshend reportedly loved it and was surprised the public didn't like it even more.
Flip the record over: the B-side is a live, unedited take on Marvin Gaye's 'Baby Don't You Do It,' recorded at San Francisco's Civic Auditorium on December 13, 1971.
That buzzing intro sound had quite the session: Townshend built it with an ARP synthesizer and a Lowrey Berkshire organ — the same Lowrey heard on 'Baba O'Riley' and 'Won't Get Fooled Again.'

The video, shot in June 1972, is the band miming to playback for an excited crowd. Daltrey and Keith Moon play Jew's harps, while Townshend and John Entwistle mime Townshend's chord and bass harmonica parts.
End of an era on the label: this was the last Who single released in the United States using Decca's old color-bar label design.
On the 1975–76 tour it became a jam vehicle, played slower and stretched out alongside 'Naked Eye,' 'Roadrunner' and 'My Generation.' Decades later, in 2008, Nissan used it in Maxima commercials.

title: Join Together

description: The opening track of Treasures from the Temple (2018), Thievery Corporation's companion LP to Temple of I & I — a dubby, dancehall-rooted instrumental from the duo's sessions in Jamaica.

pops.text: First track, first statement: 'San San Rock' opens Treasures from the Temple, the 2018 companion LP to Thievery Corporation's Temple of I & I.
The album arrived April 20, 2018 on ESL Music, collecting 12 original recordings and remixes from the Temple sessions. This one runs 4:05.
Those sessions happened at Geejam Studios in Port Antonio, Jamaica — the duo decamped there to soak up the island's music firsthand.
The duo is Rob Garza and Eric Hilton, who formed Thievery Corporation in the summer of 1995 at Washington, D.C.'s Eighteenth Street Lounge, bonding over dub, bossa nova and jazz records.
ESL Music is their own label — Eighteenth Street Lounge Music, named for the club where they met, and home to their records since the 1990s.
Press for the album called 'San San Rock' and 'Destroy the Wicked' treasured rarities echoing the band's dancehall-influenced past.
Temple of I & I, the album this one companions, was billed as chart-topping and was the duo's tenth studio album, recorded in Jamaica after their bossa nova detour, Saudade.
Tempo check: cataloguers clock 'San San Rock' at a very unhurried 76 BPM. This rock rocks slowly, on purpose.
A favorite moment, per a highlighted fan note on the band's Bandcamp page: that addictive drum fill — teased at 0:23 and 1:13 before the main event lands at 2:27.
It works live, too: at Brooklyn Bowl Philadelphia in March 2024, 'San San Rock' turned up at the business end of the setlist, in the closing run of the show.

title: San San Rock
